title: Immune signals change excitability
objective: Explain how inflammatory cytokines sensitize nociceptors.

steps.title: Turning up the neuron
steps.body: Inflammatory cytokines (e.g. TNF, IL-6) act on [[nociceptor|nociceptors]] to **lower their threshold** — a form of [[peripheral sensitization]]. So an immune signal literally makes the neuron fire to milder stimuli, tying inflammation to pain.

steps.prompt: What's a direct effect of inflammatory cytokines on a nociceptor?
options: They lower its firing threshold, so milder stimuli now excite it
They convert it into a fast, low-threshold touch fiber instead
They sever the neuron's connection to the spinal cord entirely
They raise its threshold, numbing the inflamed area completely
steps.explanation: Cytokines sensitize the ending (lower threshold), so normally innocuous stimuli now fire it — the immune-to-pain link.

variants.setup: TNF and IL-6 bathe a nociceptor ending during inflammation.
options: It drops, so weaker stimuli fire it
variants.reveal: Inflammatory cytokines lower the nociceptor's threshold (sensitization).

steps.setup: You block the receptor for a key inflammatory cytokine on sensory neurons, during inflammation.
steps.prompt: What do you predict for pain sensitivity?
options: Reduced sensitization, if that cytokine was driving it
Stronger pain than there was before the blocking
Permanent loss of all sensation from the area
No change, if the sensitization is driven centrally instead
steps.reveal: If the cytokine was sensitizing the neuron, removing its receptor should blunt the sensitization — a direct test, and the rationale behind cytokine-blocking pain therapies.

variants.prompt: Blocking an inflammatory cytokine's receptor on neurons should…
options: Reduce the sensitization if it was driving it
Increase the pain rather than reduce it
Erase all sensation from the whole area
variants.explanation: Removing the receptor cuts the sensitizing signal.

sources.citation: Wallrapp A & Chiu IM, 2024, Annu Rev Immunol
sources.note: Review of bidirectional neuroimmune interactions in the intestine.
